summary:
"Eleven Days" — what we developed. A psychological simulator of an 11-day space expedition. The player is an observer and dispatcher — not a crew member, not a psychologist. They manage the schedule, environment and 60-minute evening budget of a four-person crew, read biographies and indicators, keep an observation journal, and turn diagnoses into mission efficiency.


How it addresses the challenge. The game reproduces real mission life — work blocks, meals, sleep, noise, privacy, scheduled contact with Earth — through real ISS-type systems: the Electron oxygen generator, CO₂ scrubber, ammonia thermal loop, CubeLab, POLARIS bio-cameras, Bio-Monitor and the Pele dosimeter. The core loop links observation to deduction: behavioural markers feed four profiles where hypotheses are excluded only by contradiction and re-checked against instruments each morning.


Why it matters. It shows that psychological atmosphere is a mission-critical resource: losing a person costs more than losing a resource. Built with TypeScript and data-driven rule tables.
details:
What it does and how it works.
"Eleven Days" is a browser-based simulator of a full expedition cycle. The player runs an 11-day schedule divided into a daily grid — wake-up, breakfast and briefing, three work blocks (A/B/C), meals, free time, a 60-minute evening budget, personal time and sleep. Four crew members — commander Sergey Vlasov, flight engineer Mark Orlov, scientist Anna Kovalyova, and pilot-medic Dmitry Sokolov — follow biographically-driven routines while their needs (sleep, food, stress, isolation, morale, trust) tick forward.

The player's levers are indirect: they edit the schedule, choose evening actions from a catalogue of 13 (heart-to-heart talks, tabletop games, recognition, private PPC conference with Mission Control, quiet module, early lights-out), and run conversations through typed dialogue lines (fact, empathy, challenge, personal, special) whose availability itself is diagnostic — a missing option means a person can no longer, not won't.

The brain of the game is the observation journal: a fact tape plus four deduction profiles with checkbox signs and 6–8 hypotheses each (28 total). Hypotheses are excluded only by a contradiction sign, never by absent data; morning re-checks restore instrument-backed exclusions. Verified diagnoses convert into KPD bonuses and points.

Benefits.

  • Teaches clinical reasoning: trigger versus cause, through consequence rather than description.
  • Makes behavioural monitoring tangible — NASA's own practice of mood questionnaires and observation logs becomes a playable loop.
  • Demonstrates real station hardware and routine as narrative objects, not decoration.
  • Failure is content: a wrong diagnosis produces a meaningful epilogue, not a game over.

Intended impact.
Players leave with three ideas: behaviour is data, not judgement; help must fit the person; and a professional strength under load becomes a vulnerability. For education, it shows that game mechanics can carry psychological knowledge more precisely than a lecture. The design scales from a playable three-day slice to the full 11-day mission.

Tools, languages, hardware, software.
TypeScript engine and UI · JSON configuration files (one per crew member, one per instrument set, one per hypothesis table) · utility-scoring behaviour rules (priorities 100→10 in a single chooseState) · deterministic simulation ticks (one tick = one minute, explicit seed for events) · deduction engine with recomputeVersions / tryExclude · acceptance test suite · web panels (station map, crew panel, report card, evening budget, dialogue modal, observation journal, morning card, final summary). Runs in any modern browser; no special hardware.

How it is creative.

  • Instruments as narrative: every real system (Electron, scrubber, thermal loop, Bio-Monitor, dosimeter, CubeLab) carries its purpose, servicing procedure and failure mode.
  • Absence of a dialogue option as a diagnostic signal — reading the menu, not the answer.
  • Morning as a verdict: instruments don't lie, hypotheses do.
  • Four dialogue sequences, each broken in its own way, derived from biography rather than a universal template.
  • A single loop stitching four levels — cycle, crew, diagnosis, economy — that existing games keep separate (ONI and RimWorld have no deduction; Phasmophobia has no crew or economy).

Factors the team considered.
Scope discipline: four crew, 11 days and a full economy were kept because the loop, not the volume, carries the idea. Ethics: vulnerability is framed as an ordinary consequence of professional commitment; no real person is depicted; nothing in the game is medical advice. Education without lectures: every educational claim is tied to a mechanic. Branding: no NASA logos, flags, mission patches or identifiers are used. Scientific claims are cited to primary public sources, and numerical values are declared as game assumptions.
